Between 1893 and 1894, a seven-member commission was appointed to investigate the effects of cannabis use on the local population in country X, in response to concern within the legislature that widespread consumption of the substance was causing a public health and social crisis. Over the course of its work, the commission examined 1,193 witnesses from various strata of society and produced a report running to seven volumes and over 3,000 pages. Its conclusions were remarkable for the era. Moderate use of the substance was found to have 'no injurious effects' on the user, whether physical or mental. Occasional excess was judged 'harmless in the great majority of cases'. Any move toward total prohibition of the substance was declared 'totally unjustifiable'. The report was nevertheless largely shelved and its recommendations ignored, both by the administration of the day and, decades later, by the independent successor state, which in 1985 enacted Y, a sweeping piece of legislation that criminalized most forms of the substance.
